articles.title: Urgent plan needed to end 'corridor care' for children, health secretary says
articles.summary: Yvette Cooper also announces £140m investment in England's urgent care system, ahead of winter.
articles.body:
The NHS must take urgent action to stop children receiving treatment in hospital corridors, Health Secretary Yvette Cooper has told the BBC.

Cooper told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg she has asked NHS England to draw up urgent plans to eliminate what is known as "corridor care" for children as a priority, and to introduce new standards for how children should be treated at A&E.

It comes after more than a dozen health groups urged the health secretary to take action to end corridor care.

The number of people waiting more than 12 hours in A&E departments from a decision to admit to actually being admitted stood at 50,582 in September, up from 44,951 in August.

Cooper said the way this data is collected will be changed to have the number of children included in the figures.

"I'm clear that child health needs to be a much greater priority for the NHS," says Cooper.

The government has an aim of ending corridor care more broadly by the end of this parliament, she added.

Kuenssberg highlighted the case of Finlay Roberts, a two-year-old boy who died in 2024 after spending the final hours of his life in a crowded A&E corridor.

Finlay's father David Roberts told the BBC the situation was a "terrible mess", with the family briefly moved into a room with a bed before being moved back into the corridor.

"He just clung to me, as we now know, slowly dying," he said.

Liz Roberts, Finlay's mother, said corridor care "robs people of their dignity when they are at their most vulnerable". She recalled being told to administer a suppository to Finlay in the corridor because there was no other option.

After hearing their story, Cooper apologised to Finlay's parents on behalf of the NHS.

"No child should be treated in a corridor. No patient should be treated in a corridor," she said.

The Whittington Health NHS Trust where this happened said they extended their condolences to Finlay's family.

They said they continue to experience periods of exceptional demand across emergency care and at times some patients may receive care in temporary clinical areas, including corridors.

They said: "Our staff work tirelessly to provide safe and compassionate care in extremely challenging conditions."

On Friday, 16 health groups - including Age UK, Marie Curie and the Royal College of Nursing (RCN) - sent a letter to Cooper, urging her to take action on ending corridor care.

It said the practice is fundamentally incompatible with NHS care standards and it would require "whole-system action" to eradicate it.

Before speaking to Kuenssberg, Cooper had warned the NHS was facing a more challenging winter than normal, after multiple heatwaves led to its busiest summer on record in England.

She announced £140m funding to boost urgent care capacity as part of an effort to deal with the impact of seasonal illnesses, including flu and norovirus.

The money will go towards 14 schemes across England, including new urgent care centres, ambulance fleets and upgrades to emergency departments.

Shadow health secretary Damian Hinds said the government needed to act, but asked it to explain where the money was coming from, while the Royal College of Nursing (RCN) England said the funding was "just another sticking plaster".

In a statement, Cooper said: "Winter will be more challenging for our NHS this year, after such a heavy summer.

"That's why we have been preparing early and investing in extra urgent care capacity to help get patients the care they need."

It comes after almost 7.3 million people attended A&E between June and August in England, according to NHS data, the highest ever figure for a summer period.

Health thinktank the King's Fund warned that the service was facing a "twin crisis" going into the winter, with little time between peak periods for staff and the system to recover.

NHS leaders are urging eligible people to get flu vaccinations, with medical director Prof Frankie Swords saying there were "ominous" signs of winter pressure already affecting hospitals.

Swords said earlier this month there were more patients coming to A&E with flu and other respiratory viruses than usual for this time of year.

"And unfortunately, people are still waiting longer than we would like them to," she added.

RCN England's executive director Patricia Marquis said the extra money was welcome in the short term but would ultimately provide "just another sticking plaster on a system that is at breaking point".

"The nursing workforce needed to deliver these services goes into winter already running on empty and short of staff," she said.

The waiting list for routine hospital treatment in England rose for the second month in a row, according to the latest data.

An estimated 7.37 million treatments were waiting to be carried out at the end of August, relating to 6.24 million patients.

These were the highest numbers since October 2025, and have raised questions as to whether the NHS will meet the government's target to treat 92% of patients within 18 weeks by 2029.

articles.title: Why Iran-US negotiations keep failing
articles.summary: Relations between the two countries are dominated by policy complexes shaped by a history of hostility.
articles.body:
Since the start of the war, there have been several negotiation initiatives between the United States and Iran. Only one – the memorandum of understanding signed in Islamabad on June 18 – was concluded, but it collapsed within days.

While prevailing analyses tend to explain this failure through the details of the provisions, this article proceeds from a different premise: that the diplomatic stalemate between the two sides is shaped by a syndrome that has governed US-Iranian relations for years.

In international relations, psychological syndromes can arise as a result of deep crises that leave their mark on political consciousness and memory, potentially obstructing efforts at rapprochement and negotiation between countries.

In the case of Iran and the US, the syndrome is comprised of two complexes: the complex Washington developed as a result of the 1979 siege of the US embassy in Tehran and the complex Tehran developed as a result of historical US hostility and its withdrawal from the Iran nuclear deal in 2018.

The roots of the rupture between the two countries go as far back as August 1953 when US and British intelligence agencies helped overthrow the nationalist government of Mohammad Mosaddegh after it nationalised the oil industry in 1951. Since then, a perception has become entrenched in Iranian consciousness: that Washington does not accept an independent government in Tehran and it is prepared to sabotage it if it goes against its interests.

From this perspective, Washington’s decision to host Shah Reza Pahlavi, who had just been overthrown by his people, for medical treatment in October 1979 was read in revolutionary Tehran as a prelude to a second coup.

Iranian students stormed the US embassy on November 4 that year and held 52 Americans for 444 days. Diplomatic relations between the two countries were severed and have not been restored to this day.

While the incident is portrayed in the Iranian narrative as a defence of the revolution, in American consciousness, it established the image of Iran as a state that does not respect international norms, whose word cannot be relied upon and whose behaviour should not be rewarded.

That is the embassy siege complex. It is not about the incident itself so much as the informal rule it produced in US decision-making: that Iran must concede first and its concession must be verified before it receives anything in return.

The Iranian complex was shaped by this history as well, but it reached its peak in May 2018 when US President Donald Trump withdrew from the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) despite the International Atomic Energy Agency’s (IAEA’s) confirmation that Tehran was complying with it.

Just two weeks later, US Secretary of State Mike Pompeo announced 12 demands for a new deal, only four of which were related to the nuclear file. Seven of them were related to Iran’s regional behaviour in Lebanon, Palestine, Iraq, Yemen, Syria, Afghanistan and the Gulf. In other words, Washington did not merely revoke an existing agreement; it also raised the ceiling of its conditions for any future agreement.

The knot then deepened in June 2025 when the US took part in the Twelve-Day War and struck the nuclear facilities at Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan at a time when a new round of indirect negotiations was scheduled in Muscat. It then reached its furthest point with Washington’s participation alongside Israel in the current war.

Accordingly, a conviction became entrenched in the Iranian consciousness that an American signature guarantees nothing, that any agreement can be overturned with a change of administration and indeed that negotiation itself may be a cover for war rather than an alternative to it.

The informal rule this has produced in Iranian decision-making is that there will be no step taken before binding guarantees and no concession before pressure is lifted.

Thus, the two complexes stand at opposite ends: The first requires Iranian action before an American quid pro quo while the second requires an American guarantee before Iranian action.

A reading of the recent negotiation initiatives shows that every US initiative bears the imprint of the embassy siege complex. The 15-point plan put forward in March demanded the dismantling of the Natanz, Isfahan and Fordow facilities; an end to uranium enrichment; the suspension of Iran’s missile programme; and the abandonment of its allies in exchange for promises to lift sanctions later.

The May draft by White House envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner linked the release of Iran’s frozen funds to the suspension of enrichment first. The American response in September also stipulated the freezing of enrichment and the entry of inspectors throughout the negotiation period.

What remains constant in the American initiatives is that Iranian action precedes the quid pro quo and verification precedes trust.

The imprint of the JCPOA withdrawal complex in the Iranian initiatives is also a constant. The five-point response in late March demanded guarantees that war would not be repeated. The 10 points put forward in April demanded a binding UN Security Council resolution shielding any agreement from being overturned. And the 14 points in May demanded a nonaggression pledge that includes Israel.

Meanwhile, the seven-day plan proposed by Tehran last month stipulated the lifting of sanctions and the US naval blockade on Iran before the opening of the Strait of Hormuz on the sixth day and the start of nuclear negotiations on the seventh. What remains constant in the Iranian initiatives is that guarantees precede action and the lifting of pressure precedes Iranian concessions.

All these initiatives were dialogue between two complexes with each side drafting its text to protect itself from a repetition of its historical experience with the other, rather than to meet the other halfway. This may explain why the gap in substance has narrowed, but the gap in trust has not.

The Islamabad memorandum represents the exception that proves the rule as it was the closest moment to a settlement because it was formulated to reassure both sides over their core concerns. To reassure Washington, it stipulated the dilution of Iran’s stockpile of enriched uranium and made the lifting of sanctions and unfreezing of funds conditional on Iranian implementation.

To reassure Tehran, it provided for an end to hostilities, respect for mutual sovereignty, a mechanism to monitor implementation and UN Security Council approval of the final agreement. Ballistic missiles were also entirely absent from the text.

But this agreement did not hold. Tehran suspended its participation in the Geneva round of talks because of the absence of a ceasefire in Lebanon, which had been a consistent demand in every Iranian initiative since March. In the Iranian reading, Washington’s inability to rein in Israel confirmed that an American signature was not enough. The JCPOA withdrawal complex immediately kicked in, and the two sides returned to square one.

By late September, the dispute appeared to have shifted definitively from substance to sequencing. Informed sources indicated that it now revolves around the order of steps rather than their content and the stated goal has become a return to an enhanced version of the June memorandum.

Here the two complexes appear in their clearest form: Washington wants the Strait of Hormuz opened and enrichment frozen first because it does not trust Iran while Tehran wants the naval blockade lifted first because it does not trust the US.

A comparison between Pompeo’s 2018 conditions and the June 2026 memorandum shows that US demands have retreated from redefining Iran’s regional role to focusing on the nuclear file and the Strait of Hormuz while Iranian demands have shifted from compensation to be paid by Washington to a conditional investment fund financed by other parties.

In other words, the substantive gap between the two sides has narrowed considerably – something that would have been unimaginable eight years ago.

However, the two complexes have not diminished; indeed, they may have deepened because of the war. Each complex feeds the other until together they have become a single syndrome, and diplomatic deadlock has turned from a passing condition into a stable structure.

Accordingly, any new formula for sequencing the steps, however precise, will remain unable to break this deadlock unless it addresses both complexes at once – something that requires a third party capable of guaranteeing both the action and the reciprocal action simultaneously.

articles.title: Boy, 14, stabbed in Manchester's Arndale Centre car park
articles.summary: Greater Manchester Police say the boy's injuries were not thought to be life threatening or life changing.
articles.body:
A 14-year-old boy has been stabbed in a car park at Manchester's Arndale Centre shopping mall.

Greater Manchester Police said the boy was injured on the 9th floor of Manchester's Arndale Centre just after 15:00 BST on Saturday.

The force said his injuries were not believed to be life threatening or life changing. The Arndale was closed for several hours after the stabbing.

Det Insp Sam Jones said: "This is believed to be an isolated incident with no risk to the wider public."

The BBC understands a row with other males had taken place beforehand.

No arrests have been made in connection with the stabbing so far and inquiries were continuing.

articles.title: Police officer shot in foot in Nottingham city centre
articles.summary: A firearm has been recovered by officers after a man and a woman fled the scene, detectives say.
articles.body:
A police officer is being treated in hospital after being shot in Nottingham city centre.

Nottinghamshire Police said the officer had approached two suspects in Angel Row shortly before 04:50 BST on Sunday.

The officer is now being treated for a wound to his foot, the force added.

Detectives said a firearm was recovered and that two suspects, a man and a woman, fled the scene.

Angel Row is currently closed and a large police scene remains in place.

Police cars are parked along the road, which is lined by fast food stores and shops, and orange traffic cones have been laid out alongside items left on the road.

The cordon has also been extended to St James's Street, where an officer is standing guard.

Assistant Chief Constable Claire Rukas said: "This is a shocking incident and a sobering reminder of the potential dangers faced by officers as they work to protect and serve the public.

"As we investigate what happened and work to apprehend the individuals involved, my thoughts today are with the injured officer, his family and colleagues.

"I also ask that anyone with additional information shares this with us without delay. Even the smallest bit of information could make all the difference to this investigation."

Neghat Khan, leader of Nottingham City Council, said she was "deeply shocked and saddened" by news of the shooting.

"My thoughts and full support are with the injured police officer, their family, and their colleagues across Nottinghamshire Police," she added.

​"Nottingham City Council is working tirelessly alongside the police to support the investigation and ensure those responsible are swiftly caught and brought to justice.

​"While incidents of this nature are extremely rare, our commitment to keeping Nottingham safe is absolute.

"Thanks to the daily bravery of our police and community protection officers, Nottingham remains a safe city, and residents can be assured that every available resource is being deployed."

In a post on social media, Nadia Whittome, MP for Nottingham East, encouraged anyone with information to contact the police.

"My thoughts are with the injured police officer and his family following this truly shocking incident," she wrote.

articles.title: Why metal detecting is booming in the age of social media and AI
articles.summary: Metal detecting enthusiasts say the hobby helps them escape the digital world and slow down.
articles.body:
In an age dominated by screens, social media and artificial intelligence (AI), metal detecting enthusiasts say the hobby helps them escape the digital world and slow down.

For cousins Lucilla Gray and Eleanor Bruce, what started as a hobby during the Covid pandemic evolved into a way to switch off from modern life's constant distractions.

The pair, from Lincolnshire, have been metal detecting for six years.

In that time they have uncovered Roman brooch fragments, a Medieval buckle and a Victorian needle casing with an incredible women's history tied to it.

But for them, the appeal is more than finding treasure. It is about escaping screens, spending time outdoors and being present in the moment.

"If you struggle with your mental health, I think metal detecting can really help with grounding, giving you focus," Lucilla, 34, says.

"It helps to stop overthinking things and you have to be really present in what you're doing. It's a good way to give your brain a bit of a break."

Eleanor says people are returning to more nostalgic hobbies, like metal detecting, to combat the fast-paced world of social media and artifical intelligence (AI).

"There is quite a trend at the minute for returning to what people deem as being nostalgic hobbies," the 27-year-old says.

"I think metal detecting is certainly one of them - it's like all the people still shooting on 35 millimetre film.

"There's this massive trend of going back in time because our world is developing and expanding so rapidly with social media and AI."

Alan Tamblyn, general secretary of the National Council for Metal Detecting (NCMD), said the pastime is becoming increasingly popular, with about 50,000 people taking part, compared to 20,000 about five years ago.

According to the Portable Antiquities Scheme (PAS) , there were nearly 80,000 finds recorded in 2024. Metal detectorists accounted for 94% of all recorded finds.

Alan believes its growing popularity is being fuelled by an increasing interest in history, as well as a desire to step away from the pressures of modern society.

"You're re-engaging with nature, you've got the fresh air, you're just switching off and listening to the bird song," he says. "Being out in the middle of nowhere on a sunny day is quite something."

Alan explains the hobby's appeal has also widened beyond its traditional audience of older men, with more families and women getting involved.

Lucilla agrees: "Stereotypically, metal detecting, and also being interested in history, is very male-dominated.

"It's really important to have more women's voices in these spaces and also telling stories of some of the finds and history that maybe wouldn't be spotlighted because it's coming from two younger women."

The pair, who call themselves Roman Found on social media, even wrote a book called Things We Found in the Ground, detailing their journey.

In the book, they explain one of their finds was a needle casing which depicts a portrait of Princess Helena.

She was one of the founders of the Royal School of Needlework which empowered women at the beginning of the suffrage.

Despite attracting increasing numbers of people, Alan says metal detecting is more than just a hobby, it is about rewriting history.

"The things that we find like medieval coins, Roman coins, artefacts, Medieval, brooches and buckles - all of those items tell a story and they are part of our shared national heritage," he says.

One person who has contributed to Lincolnshire's national heritage is Rafal Wesolowski from Boston.

The 50-year-old unearthed a rare early medieval silver-gilt finger ring with a runic inscription in a field in Quadring in South Holland in May 2024.

Rafal reported the find to the PAS and experts from the University of Nottingham had confirmed its early medieval date and importance.

Archaeologist Dr Lisa Brundle described it as one of "the most significant" archaeological finds ever recorded in the area.

Despite the rare ring being one of his favourite finds, he says the recognition and helping shape local history, it is not why he does what he does.

Rafal says he loves metal detecting because it helps him slow down.

Growing up loving sport and being busy, he says it helps him stay calm and encourages him to do engage in other mindful hobbies like reading books about the artefacts he has found.

"Finding new coins, new artefacts makes me happy," he says. "I read more history and get more excited about what I find."

He adds: "One day at an event for metal detectors... I remember sleeping in a tent, waking up early, everybody sleeps, making a coffee.

"I see the mountain, little bees, the forest and the field... this is beautiful."

As well as helping them get away from screens, the hobby also brought Eleanor, who grew up in Lincolnshire, and Lucilla, who grew up in New Zealand, together.

"I think being able to reconnect with that side of my family and heritage was quite important in finding somewhere to belong," Lucilla, who has now moved back to Lincolnshire, says.

Alan adds: "Once people get into it, it really is a community. It really is a family.

"One question we get asked a lot is, 'what's the best thing we've discovered?' I can honestly say, cheesy as it is, the biggest thing and most important thing that I found while in my 28 years of metal detecting is the people.

"I've met some amazing people and that continues."

articles.title: A Utah couple wanted a place to scuba without travelling, so they built a $2 million, 360,000-gallon backyard pool with a 90-foot mountain, five waterfalls, a 300-foot lazy river and a 26-foot-deep diving tunnel
articles.summary: A Utah couple wanted a place where they could practise scuba diving without travelling to the ocean.
articles.body: A Utah couple wanted a place where they could practise scuba diving without travelling to the ocean. Their solution was to build a $2 million backyard swimming pool with 360,000 gallons of water, a 90-foot man-made mountain, five waterfalls and an underwater tunnel that takes divers down to a depth of 26 feet. Called “The Mountain”, the pool was built at a home in Springville, Utah. It stretches 140 feet long and 60 feet wide, and includes a 300-foot lazy river, a hidden grotto, winding pathways and a water slide concealed inside the mountain.As reported by FOX 13 News, the unusual pool was featured on Animal Planet’s television programme ‘The Pool Master,’ hosted by pool designer Anthony Archer-Wills. The project was designed for a homeowner who loved mountains and scuba diving, the broadcaster reported.A 90-foot mountain in the backyardThe pool’s main feature is a 90-foot artificial mountain designed to resemble the natural landscape around the property. It includes five waterfalls, several hidden pathways and two bridges that wind towards the top. Archer-Wills described the structure as one that “emulates the natural surroundings perfectly”, according to FOX 13 News. The mountain is not just decorative. A hidden water slide runs for 60 feet through the structure before dropping into the pool below. There is also a secluded grotto tucked behind the waterfalls, giving swimmers another place to explore. The pool’s design combines these features with a 300-foot lazy river, allowing the owners to swim, float and explore different parts of the property without leaving home.A tunnel that lets the owners practise scuba divingScuba diving was one of the main reasons the couple commissioned the pool. Utah is far from the ocean, so having a deep-water area at home offered them a place to practise. According to FOX 13 News, a concealed entrance inside the mountain leads to a tunnel measuring 54 feet long and five feet wide. The tunnel reaches a depth of 26 feet and connects to the main pool. The underwater section is intended for scuba-certified divers. It allows them to put on diving equipment and practise underwater skills without travelling to a coastal diving location. As reported by Scuba Diving magazine, the $2 million project included the 54-foot tunnel, five waterfalls, the lazy river and a hidden 60-foot slide in the year 2014.A kitchen, bridges and hidden spacesThe pool also has facilities for spending time outdoors beyond swimming and diving. According to FOX 13 News, the mountain houses a full kitchen with granite countertops, stainless-steel cabinets, a refrigerator and an eight-burner grill. The bridges and paths offer access to the upper sections of the structure, while the hidden grotto and winding passages give the mountain several enclosed spaces to explore. The combination of water features, diving facilities and kitchen space makes the backyard pool more elaborate than a conventional residential swimming pool.A $2 million project featured on televisionThe project came to wider attention when it appeared on ‘The Pool Master,’ a programme that follows pool designer Anthony Archer-Wills as he transforms residential outdoor spaces. The pool cost approximately $2 million to build. In its 2015 report, Scuba Diving magazine highlighted the project as an example of how a private swimming pool could be designed around a specific hobby. For the Utah homeowners, the central purpose was practical as well as recreational: they wanted somewhere to practise scuba diving close to home. articles.title: Photos: Protests across France spiral into looting, blazes and clashes
articles.summary: Authorities report 1,200 arrests and 150 injured police officers as unrest erupts in multiple French cities.
articles.body:
France woke up on Sunday to streets scarred by burned cars, smashed shopfronts and looted businesses after cost-of-living protests spiralled into some of the worst unrest in years.

What began as largely peaceful marches on Saturday over soaring prices and falling living standards quickly escalated, with masked youths torching vehicles, ransacking shops and attacking public buildings in cities including Paris, Marseille, Nice, Bordeaux, Lille and Strasbourg.

Paris Deputy Mayor Emmanuel Gregoire said “whole streets have been devastated” as police used tear gas and water cannon against protesters who hurled projectiles and set off fireworks. Authorities reported about 1,200 arrests and 150 injured police officers. It was “a miracle the toll isn’t higher,” Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said.

Town halls in Limoges, Marseille and Lille were targeted, while a police compound in Bordeaux and a tourist office in Lyon were vandalised. In Saint-Etienne, a 17-year-old lost his right hand after being hit by a crowd-control grenade.

The unrest follows weeks of student protests to demand more investment in education and comes six months before the presidential election. Far-right and left-wing contenders traded blame over the violence, even as President Emmanuel Macron promised that those responsible for looting and attacks on public buildings “will be prosecuted and punished”.

images.caption: Violent clashes, fires and looting marred demonstrations across France on October 17, 2026, as hundreds of thousands of people marched against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools. [Stephanie Lecocq/Reuters]

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said 110 marches drew about 550,000 people across the country, while organisers, including the CGT labour union and student organisations, put the figure at about 800,000. [Geoffroy Van Der Hasselt/AFP]

Nunez describes troublemakers as “extremely violent, radical far-left groups” seeking confrontations with police and targeting public buildings, joined by offenders willing to loot shops; most of those arrested are adults, he says. [Dimitar Dilkoff/AFP]

After weeks of student protests, France now faces broader nationwide demonstrations over the cost of living, setting up a potentially fraught six months ahead of the presidential election. [Geoffroy Van Der Hasselt/AFP]

In Paris, police fired tear gas and water cannon to push back people wearing hoods and masks who were throwing fireworks, paving stones and other objects at officers in Republic Square, northeast of the Paris city centre. [Abdul Saboor/Reuters]
French firefighters extinguish a burning car amid clashes during nationwide "yellow vests" protests in Paris. [Stephanie Lecocq/Reuters]

articles.title: Ilkley Moor 'boulder' house approved after planning appeal
articles.summary: Town council had objected to the plans but the folklore-inspired house will now be built.
articles.body:
Plans for a house designed to look like rocks on a famous Yorkshire moor have been approved.

The contemporary structure, which has large irregular-shaped windows and a natural outdoor pool, looks similar to the landmark Cow and Calf Rocks in Ilkley, West Yorkshire.

The house will be built on green belt land which is the garden of a home off Heber's Ghyll Drive, and will be eco-friendly, to an ultra-low energy standard called Passivhaus.

Harrogate-based architects Shaw & Jagger said the scheme was eventually passed by HM Planning Inspectorate through the country house clause, which allows development on green belt for buildings of "exceptional quality".

The architect Matt Masserella-Gill was commissioned to design the home by the landowner David Rasche.

He said the design was "arguably the most complex country house application ever made in this country".

The house has been named Fomorian - meaning a supernatural race of giants in Irish mythology - taking inspiration from the mythical giant Rombald who is told to have lived on Ilkley Moor.

Masserella-Gill said: "The design approach was to propose a scheme that is intrinsically linked to the spirit of its place. Fomorian is of its place, part of the moors, its geology and its spirit.

"We took cues from local folklore, the surrounding rocks; ancient carvings, standing stones and escarpments that are synonymous with the landscape."

The application was originally submitted to Bradford Council planners, but was not passed on the grounds of non-determination - meaning a decision was not made within the required timeframe.

The plans had received an objection from Ilkley Town Council, who recommended it be refused as it would be a "visual anomaly to the moorland".

The land "forms part of the South Pennine Moors Site of Special Scientific Interest, the South Pennine Moors Special Protection Area and Special Area of Conservation, and more recently, which has been designated as a new National Nature Reserve," it said.

The council also noted the proposed development was close to the Swastika Stone, a prehistoric rock carving which is one of hundreds of Scheduled Ancient Monuments on Ilkley Moor.

Bradford Council's decision was appealed however, and was passed by the Planning Inspectorate in August.

Masserella-Gill added: "The site is subject to restrictive planning policies which made the principle of development very challenging.

The country house clause requires an isolated design of "exceptional quality" in that it "is truly outstanding", would "significantly enhance its immediate setting and be sensitive to the defining characteristics of the local area".

He said the planning inspector noted that Fomorian was "an innovative design" that "would help raise the standards of design in the rural area more generally".

articles.title: In 2020, Brazil tested sugarcane bagasse ash in a highway resurfacing; a 2023 inspection found no visible defects in either section, while lab wheel tests showed 11% less deformation in the ash mixture
articles.summary: Brazil's recent study reveals that replacing mineral filler with sugarcane ash in asphalt can reduce rutting by 11%, showing promise for more sustainable road construction.
articles.body: The surfaces of asphalt roads degrade in an irregular pattern depending on traffic. Vehicles with heavy loads repeatedly drive along the same small path, slowly forming grooves that are called ruts in the road surface. Road administrations pay lots of money to repair those areas, whereas engineers try to find suitable asphalt mixes that would not degrade in the first place. Sugarcane milling provides one of the possible ingredients. Mills burn bagasse, a byproduct of sugar juice production, into ash, which is disposed of somewhere.The 2024 Maringá studyVinicius Milhan Hipólito and Jesner Sereni Ildefonso studied the use of sugarcane bagasse ash in asphalt pavement in Functional and structural assessment of an experimental section gap graded modified with sugarcane bagasse ash, published in Scientific Reports on 8 August 2024. The study examined an experimental section of the BR-158 highway in Paraná, Brazil, constructed in September 2020. The reference mixture was a gap-graded asphalt with a rubber-modified binder and in the modified mixture, the ash made up 5% of the total mineral aggregates, replacing conventional filler. The researchers found that 5% was the maximum proportion that kept the mixture within the recommended grain-size range.The BR-158 test sectionThe experimental section was on the BR-158 highway in Paraná. The existing asphalt surface was milled and covered with a 10 cm layer of dense-graded mix and then a 3.5 cm layer of gap-graded mix. The first 60 metres received the ash mixture and the next 60 metres received the standard mixture under the toll company’s maintenance programme, so both sections carried the same traffic.Laboratory tests and the May 2023 inspectionSamples taken from the experimental lane were tested in the Hamburg Wheel Tracking Device, which rolls a loaded steel wheel across each sample under water. The test ran at 50 °C with a 705 N wheel load for 20,000 revolutions. The reference mixture deformed by 3.6 mm and the ash mixture by 3.2 mm, which is 11% less. Both mixtures stayed below the 4 mm threshold the authors used as an indicator of adequate properties.A second laboratory test, dynamic creep, also favoured the ash mixture. It showed 28% less deformation after 10,000 cycles and a flow number of 16,707 against 9,681 for the reference mixture, which is 73% higher. A road inspection in May 2023 found no visible surface defects on either section. Because the reference section was also free of defects, this shows the ash section held up under traffic but does not show that it outperformed the reference mixture.A 2026 laboratory study of ash in asphalt masticA separate team tested the same material in the binder. Prasad Bishetti and Aniket Kataware’s study, Valorization of Sugarcane Bagasse Ash for Sustainable Asphalt Mastics: Material Characterization and Performance Evaluation, appeared in the Journal of Transportation Engineering, Part B: Pavements in 2026. In this laboratory study of mastics, not a road test, the ash replaced granite filler at 0% to 25% by mass. The best results came at 15% to 20% replacement, where non-recoverable creep compliance, an indicator of rutting susceptibility, fell by 79% and fatigue life rose 1.18 times.What the evidence supports so farTaken together, these two studies support only a limited conclusion. Bagasse ash can replace part of the mineral filler without degrading performance, at least in the laboratory tests and on one heavily trafficked road during the first inspection period. Neither study shows that the ash prevents rutting over a pavement’s whole service life. The field test also covered only 120 metres, of which 60 used the ash mixture. The authors of the above-mentioned study concluded that partially replacing conventional filler with the ash is technically feasible in both laboratory and field settings. Further observation is needed before agencies adopt the ash as a filler in their pavements. The mastic study also replaced filler at much higher shares than the 5% of total aggregate used on the BR-158, so the two figures are not directly comparable.You use AI every day. articles.title: Exmoor pony herd gathering raises money for air ambulance
articles.summary: Kristina Auckland said the herd was made up of around 100 ponies.
articles.body:
A herd of ponies on Exmoor is being gathered as part of an annual inspection.

Tippbarlake Exmoor Pony Herd has about 100 ponies, which are being gathered in Brendon Barton on Sunday.

Kristina Auckland, who looks after the herd with her family, said gathering ponies on Exmoor was a tradition that had been going on for generations.

She said members of the public were able to watch at Scobhill Gate from 10:00 for free but would be asked to donate to the Devon Air Ambulance.

Auckland said the ponies lived freely on Brendan Common and "we try and manage them from afar all year round".

"Once a year we will gather them in to have a bit of a closer inspection and make sure that they're all healthy and their welfare needs are met," she added.

The numbers of people watching the gathering had "steadily increased" over the last few years, which Auckland attributed to the rise of social media.

She added there were also many local families who came to watch yearly.

Auckland said they had chosen to collect donations for Devon Air Ambulance this year because it was "absolutely crucial" for people in rural communities.

"We're completely reliant on the air ambulance being able to help us, whether you're a farmer, a local resident, or someone visiting," she said.

She added: "Whatever anyone's able to donate, as as little or as much as possible is amazing."

Auckland said she wanted to "raise awareness of the breed and the role the ponies play in managing the common itself and what they can contribute to conservation projects around the country," she said.

"They are born to eat ... and they're really good at eating certain types of grasses and sort of managing habitats."

She added: "They're a really important part of Exmoor's heritage and we're so lucky to have many herds still living freely on the moor.

"We want people to understand their value and the role they play, and we want them to be here for generations to come."

articles.title: Ukrainian drone attack on Russia’s St Petersburg kills 1, hits energy sites
articles.summary: Zelenskyy says Russian attacks on Ukraine overnight kill two people, adding that Moscow continues to break energy ceasefire.
articles.body:
A “massive” Ukrainian drone attack on St Petersburg in Russia has killed at least one person and injured five others, the city’s governor said on Sunday.

Alexandre Beglov said firefighters were battling blazes at the St Petersburg oil terminal, the Ruchi oil depot and industrial warehouses in the Kolpino district south of the city.

The governor said several residential buildings were also hit, along with two houses.

City authorities said the attack disrupted flights at St Petersburg’s main airport, one of the country’s busiest, which was restricting operations “for safety reasons”, Beglov said.

Russian e-commerce company Ozon said there was a fire at its logistics hub in St Petersburg, and the internet company VK said its data centre in the Leningrad region had been attacked by drones, adding that normal services were available to users.

The governor of the Leningrad region surrounding St Petersburg, Alexander Drozdenko, said 145 drones had been shot down and about 20,000 people were without electricity following the drone raid.

Russia’s state-run news agency TASS said the attack was the largest on the region in the last four years.

Moscow’s defence ministry said 1,015 Ukrainian drones were neutralised overnight.

In Ukraine, Russian forces struck residential buildings overnight, killing two people and injuring 12, including two children, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post on X on Sunday.

“This morning, there was a strike on an agricultural enterprise in Volyn. All necessary services are working at the site,” he said.

“In total, over this past week, the Russians have attacked Ukraine with almost 2,700 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs, and 66 missiles, most of them ballistic.”

The attacks came after Zelenskyy said this week that Kyiv would resume hitting Russian refineries, insisting he was standing up for his war-torn country, as support from the United States declined.

Zelenskyy told the British newspaper the Financial Times this week that Kyiv was “done” with an “energy ceasefire” unilaterally declared by United States President Donald Trump and would resume strikes on Russia in retaliation for a wave of attacks.

Trump announced an immediate “ energy ceasefire ” between Russia and Ukraine last week, but Zelenskyy said Moscow continued to violate the deal.

“Since the American President announced the energy ceasefire a week ago, Russia has deliberately attacked Ukraine’s energy and oil and gas sectors 76 times,” he wrote in his X post on Sunday.

“Last night alone, there were strikes on substations in the Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi, and Odesa regions,” he wrote, adding that tens of thousands of families remained without power as energy workers and repair crews worked round the clock to restore supplies.

Zelenskyy also said that the main targets of Moscow’s recent strikes were energy facilities, as the Russians were trying to “cause a blackout”.

“America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements,” he said.

Trump is also facing criticism in both Europe and the US after he signed an executive order on Friday to waive sanctions and tariffs targeting Moscow’s energy revenues.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday that Trump’s waiver would be a pause to “analyse” their impact on the global economy.

“The president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy,” Rubio said, noting that the economic restrictions involved a number of countries, not just Russia.

Trump said late on Saturday his decision would benefit the US.

“We’ll figure it out, and you’ll figure it out,” he said. “It’s a very good decision, and it’s going to be a decision that’s good for the country, and I think good for the world.”

articles.title: In 2018, a Queens shopper paid $1.99 each for four Picasso plates; experts authenticated all four, and four years later, three brought in $34,000 at auction in 2022
articles.summary: A shopper in Queens finds Picasso plates for $1.99 each, authenticated and sold for $34,000 at auction, showcasing the unexpected treasures in thrift stores.
articles.body: A second-hand shopping trip in Queens, New York, led Nancy Cavaliere to discover four ceramic plates inscribed with the name of Pablo Picasso. The plates were purchased for $1.99 each at a Salvation Army thrift shop, and eventually authenticated as works from the artist’s Visage Noir series. Three of them were auctioned separately in December 2022, and Cavaliere watched the sale online. According to The Guardian, the first plate reached $8,000, followed by $10,000 for the second, while the final plate sold for $16,000, bringing the total to $34,000.Finding Picasso in the homeware aisle After getting married in 2014, Cavaliere had developed a penchant for second-hand shopping while furnishing her first rented apartment. Saddled by the high cost of conventional home decor, she chose thrift stores as an alternative to look for furniture, clothing, and decorative objects. She also created an online blog to chronicle her vintage discoveries and share the experience with other thrift shoppers.In August 2018, following several weeks without finding anything, she visited a large Salvation Army shop in Queens. The clothing section did not offer anything that piqued her interest, so she headed towards the homeware aisle before leaving. Among the china, she found a plate decorated with a painted face, and its white lines and turquoise details stood out against a black background. This inspired her to envision how the plates would look when arranged on a table during formal hosting or dinners, and she decided to buy them.The pieces were in good condition, and when she turned one over at home, she noticed an indentation bearing the name Picasso. Next, she contacted a friend who worked in antiques to verify whether the indentation was credible or not. Although her friend advised her not to assume the plates were authentic, she encouraged Cavaliere to purchase them because of their distinctive appearance.Soon after, Cavaliere contacted an auction house that dealt with Picasso ceramics and sent videos along with photos for the examination. The specialist confirmed the authenticity of the plates and offered to arrange their sale, which was scheduled for years later, and according to The Guardian, the auction house valued each plate at $5,000.The ceramics behind the discovery The plates belonged to Picasso’s Visage Noir series, a collection of hand-painted ceramic works he produced in southern France while working at the Madoura pottery studio, after meeting its founders, Suzanne and Georges Ramié, as per the Vallauris town hall page. The studio was located in Vallauris and played an important part in the artist’s ceramic work, stimulating his creative exploration of forms and surfaces beyond his paintings and sculptures.For his ceramic work, Picasso used plates, dishes, bowls, and other objects and decorated them with faces, animals, and abstract designs. These works were a result of combining pottery with visual language and making art out of everyday objects. Cavaliere’s plates had the same geometric faces, which were consistent with the type of imagery that made Picasso ceramic work recognisable to collectors.Ultimately, the three plates were sold; Cavaliere retained the fourth and planned to sell it in the future and use the proceeds to benefit her daughter. The proceeds from the three plates were invested in the stock market because Cavaliere did not want the excitement of the sale to lead to impulsive spending. In May 2023, Antique Trader reported that she was keeping the fourth piece in a safety deposit box and intended to wait 20 years, until about 2043, before selling it.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘With help of God & your prayers’: Pope Leo XIV makes first public appearance after lung cancer surgery
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV made his first public appearance on Sunday since undergoing surgery for lung cancer five days ago, addressing crowds gathered in St Peter’s
articles.body: Pope Leo XIV made his first public appearance on Sunday since undergoing surgery for lung cancer five days ago, addressing crowds gathered in St Peter’s Square from a window of the Vatican’s Apostolic Palace and assuring the faithful that he would gradually return to his duties.The 71-year-old pontiff appeared unaided at the window and delivered his customary Sunday noon address in a firm, clear voice, smiling as he spoke to pilgrims gathered below under cloudy skies.Thanking people around the world for their prayers and support, Leo said he had come through a delicate phase of his recovery and would begin resuming his activities with their continued prayers and God’s help.“Having overcome this delicate phase ... I will now gradually resume my activities, always with the help of God and your prayers,” he said.He also urged pilgrims to put aside selfish ambitions and serve God “without compromise”.The appearance marked Leo’s first public engagement since he underwent an operation on Tuesday to remove the lower lobe of his right lung.The surgery, which came during the 71-year-old’s 17-month papacy, had raised questions about how his health might affect his ability to carry out his responsibilities as head of the Catholic Church, which has around 1.4 billion members.Pope discharged from hospital ahead of scheduleCatholic faithful gathered in St Peter’s Square to welcome Leo back after he was discharged from Rome’s Gemelli hospital on Saturday, four days after the operation.The pontiff had indicated that he was recovering well, telling a reporter in English that he was doing “much better” as he left the hospital.His discharge came earlier than the week-long hospital stay initially anticipated, AP reported.The operation confirmed that Leo had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. Tests on the tumour and related lymph nodes were underway, with the results expected to help doctors determine whether he would need further treatment.Possible treatment options include chemotherapy, a combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy, or targeted oral therapy depending on the tumour’s genetic characteristics, according to news agency AP.Next major engagement is planned for NovemberLeo’s next major engagement is an overseas trip scheduled for November 6-17, covering Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. The itinerary includes a dozen flights and two helicopter rides to high-altitude locations.His surgeon, Dr Stefano Margaritora, told Vatican News on Saturday that there were “no clinical reasons” to rule out the trip.Margaritora said the pontiff had devoted considerable effort to his recovery and was expected to recover fully from the operation in around 10 more days.The results of the ongoing tests will help determine whether any additional treatment is required as Leo continues his recovery and prepares to resume his public duties.You use AI every day. articles.title: Jordan-Israel border becomes new hotspot for sophisticated drug trade
articles.summary: A surge in drug smuggling from Israel to Jordan using drones and balloons prompts accusations of border guard collusion.
articles.body:
Amman, Jordan – Jordanians fear the country’s border with Israel is turning into a major drug-smuggling route amid a surge in high-tech operations by gangs using drones and helium-filled balloons.

Organised networks active in southern Israel’s Negev Desert have links to groups in Jordan and the Sinai Peninsula in Egypt, operating along one of the most heavily surveilled borders in the world, with Jordanian authorities increasingly concerned about the implications this could have for the kingdom.

This escalation coincides with changes in the regional drug trade, particularly after the fall of Syrian President Bashar al-Assad in late 2024.

Elements in his regime were linked to the manufacturing and distribution of Captagon, an illegal amphetamine stimulant.

Syria became a hub for the distribution of Captagon to the Gulf, with Jordan a transit point and market for the drug. The Royal Jordanian Air Force carried out periodic strikes on drug manufacturing and smuggling points inside Syria, highlighting the huge security concerns Jordan had about the trade.

Since the collapse of the Assad government and the establishment of a new authority that views the Captagon trade as a national security issue, there has been a decrease in the drug trade from Syria into Jordan.

Although Druze militias in the Syrian province of Suwayda allegedly linked to Israel have been accused of continuing the drug trade, Jordanian security forces are increasingly focused on the Jordan-Israel border.

The use of quadcopter drones and balloons is reportedly among the new tactics used by gangs in Israel to smuggle hashish, crystal meth, and amphetamines into Jordan.

Jordanian security forces are said to be increasingly unhappy with the scale of the drug smuggling operations and have accused the Israeli army of not taking the issue seriously.

Initial data from Jordanian forces recorded 17 interception operations linked to drones during the first half of 2026 in Jordan’s southwestern border area with Israel.

They also recorded 231 smuggling and infiltration attempts and downed 56 drones across various borders during the same period.

Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya told Al Jazeera that Jordanian forces were continuing efforts to prevent drugs from being smuggled into the kingdom. But they are evidently facing more complex activities by drug dealers.

“There is an increase in drug smuggling operations from Israel to Jordan using drones,” he said. “The number of seized drug cases during the current year reached 15,342 cases. Trafficking cases constituted about 28 percent of them, compared with 72 percent for usage cases.”

Israeli media reports indicate that gangs active in the Negev Desert are behind some of the smuggling operations into Jordan, where drugs can fetch higher profits.

There are estimates that 1kg of hashish can sell for approximately 7,500 pounds sterling (almost $10,000), according to the British newspaper The Telegraph, which recently uncovered the drug smugglers’ latest operations. Israeli security services believe that the price of hashish in Jordan is about 15 times higher than in Israel.

Due to widespread disenfranchisement and poverty, elements within Palestinian communities in Israel have been linked to the drug trade, according to reports. Multiple sources have accused Israel of allowing Palestinian towns and cities to become hotbeds of crime to create divisions and prevent calls for greater rights.

Ammar al-Qudah, a member of the Jordanian Senate and retired major-general in the Public Security Directorate, claimed that organised gangs in the Negev had obtained more than 1,000 drones that were originally used for agricultural and security purposes.

“The smuggling networks are linked to other gangs in Jordan, Sinai and the Negev, and rely on a route starting from Sinai, passing through the Negev, and reaching Wadi Araba, in addition to other routes including the Lebanese border with Israel and the Galilee region towards Syria,” he told Al Jazeera.

They are also using a range of sophisticated technology to bypass security on both sides of the border. This includes the use of helium-filled balloons equipped with GPS devices, drones capable of carrying about 50kg of narcotics, including black hashish and crystal meth, al-Qudah said.

He warned that a portion of the black hashish and crystal meth being smuggled into the kingdom is being sold domestically, with the rest going to other markets in the region.

With such high-tech operations, there are accusations that members of Israeli forces know about drug gang activities, based on past experiences in Egypt.

One West Point report said current and former trackers in the Israeli military in the Negev are being recruited by traffickers to provide intelligence to facilitate their operations in Egypt. In 2012, a number of Israeli service personnel were arrested on suspicion of collaborating with drug smugglers across the Egyptian border.

While there is no proof that the same situation is being repeated in Jordan, many have questioned how drones and balloons carrying drugs could cross a heavily surveilled and guarded Israeli border into Jordan.

Jordan’s counternarcotics department, in cooperation with the armed forces, has tracked such cases and made arrests.

Retired Brigadier-General Daifallah al-Daboubi, a strategic and military expert, said Jordan is witnessing a “reverse drug migration”, starting from the Sinai Peninsula, passing through the Negev region, and reaching the kingdom.

“Groups active in Beersheba and the Negev possess great financial capabilities and use advanced smuggling methods, most notably drones,” he said.

The Israeli army’s preoccupation with wars in Gaza, Lebanon and the occupied Golan Heights has provided smugglers with room to manoeuvre on the Jordan border, he added. But he ruled out the direct involvement of the Israeli political or military leadership in any drug smuggling.

Steps taken by Israel to boost security on its eastern border include the establishment of the 96th Division, which began operating in the Jordan Valley in 2025, and the construction of a controversial security barrier with Jordan.

But none of these measures appears to be designed to prevent drugs from leaving Israel; instead, they appear to be designed to prevent weapons and other illicit merchandise from entering the country from Jordan.

articles.title: NHS data breaches a disgrace, says Health Secretary Yvette Cooper
articles.summary: A total of 15 NHS staff are sacked for accessing records of the Nottingham attacks victims.
articles.body:
NHS staff accessing the medical records of the Nottingham attacks victims and possible breaches over a man killed by a tiger is a "disgrace", the health secretary has said.

Speaking to the BBC, Yvette Cooper said she expected action to be taken against staff who have breached NHS data and privacy standards.

Her comments came after Nottingham University Hospitals (NUH) NHS Trust confirmed it had sacked a total of 15 members of staff and Yorkshire Ambulance Service said William Chapman's medical records may have been accessed illegitimately.

Dr Manjeet Shehmar, NUH medical director, previously said there was "simply no excuse for accessing the records of a patient without a legitimate reason".

Speaking to the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Cooper said "there's got to be proper respect for patients" from NHS staff.

"Let me be really clear about this," she said. "There are proper data and privacy standards across the NHS.

Students Barnaby Webber and Grace O'Malley-Kumar, and grandfather Ian Coates, were stabbed to death on 13 June 2023 by Valdo Calocane, who was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020.

NUH said in May that it had sacked 11 members of staff for inappropriately accessing the victims' medical records and had informed the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) and Nottinghamshire Police of the investigation.

At the time, the ICO told the BBC it would "assess any evidence provided by the trust in due course and consider our next steps", while police said there was "no criminal investigation".

In its update about further dismissals on Friday, NUH said it had taken action against "doctors, nurses, registered healthcare professionals and other staff" and that independent regulators such as the Nursing and Midwifery Council and General Medical Council, the ICO and Nottinghamshire Police had been informed.

NUH added a new system, currently under testing, is being implemented to protect patient records in future and alert the trust to potential breaches.

Reacting to the dismissals on Saturday, Dr Sanjoy Kumar, Grace's father, said the families of the victims of the attacks would like to meet with Cooper.

He also called for action to be taken over the data breaches.

Kumar added: "I'd like to ask Yvette Cooper the question, when is this going to stop and what is she doing exactly to make this stop and decrease the suffering of people who are victims of crime and of major incidents, when is this going to stop?

"I am appalled. It's time to get a handle on these failures.

"Clearly, the way that the highest confidential data, which is medical data, is being looked at by voyeuristic people in the NHS is disgraceful."

On Friday, Yorkshire Ambulance Service said staff members may have accessed the records of William Chapman, 24, who was mauled to death by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park on 10 October.

It said an investigation had been launched "to establish the full circumstances surrounding these potential breaches".

On Thursday, an inquest into Chapman's death heard that he died as a result of "multiple traumatic injuries and animal interaction" after entering the tiger's enclosure at the park, near Doncaster.

In a statement, a spokesperson for Yorkshire Ambulance Service NHS Trust said Chapman's family was aware of the potential breach and offered their condolences to his relatives.

Cooper said: "Every member of NHS staff knows that, and every member of NHS staff needs to abide by it, and the overwhelming majority of NHS staff not only do that, they also hugely value those privacy and dignity standards.

"It is a disgrace that we've had cases where people don't, and we do expect action to be taken, including people being sacked, and I've spoken to the NHS England chief executive about this.

"We also expect where there are these breaches taking place, we expect people to be swiftly suspended while investigations take place.

"There's got to be proper respect for patients, and I think that is a core value in the NHS."

articles.title: Jeremy Vernon battles with overgrown pathways in Launceston
articles.summary: One man's battle against weeds and overgrown pathways makes a big difference to the town
articles.body:
A resident of Launceston, Cornwall, goes above and beyond battling weeds and overgrown pathways free of charge to keep fit and help the community.

Jeremy Vernon, 51, said despite having his kidney removed due to cancer he could not resist clearing neglected paths in his free time and it had made him a hit on social media.

In one area he cut back the brambles and scraped off all the weeds before spending several hours pressure washing the steps.

He said he did it due to "the satisfaction after walking down the path after it has been cleaned and the reaction you get from members of the public and people on social media that seem to appreciate what's being done".

Vernon is a self-employed steel erector who has worked on rollercoasters and movie sets, such as Death on the Nile and Ready Player One.

He had been living in Wiltshire until he discovered he had kidney cancer, had a kidney removed and moved back to Cornwall for what he called a "better, nicer pace of life".

"But work is still up London way, but when I get back down here I go for a walk see a mess get my shovel and wheelbarrow and start clearing places up.

"It keeps you fit and I think it is better than going to the gym.

"I rang Launceston Town Council, they explained the pathways are not theirs and gave me a number for Cornwall Council.

"I have rang them two or three times explaining that I have the public liability insurance but I don't have permission to be where I am so it kind of invalidates my insurance."

In a statement Cornwall Council said: "We support residents volunteering and our contractor Cormac oversees a range of community-led projects on council land, from working on woodland to re-wilding parks to weeding open spaces.

"Last year 60,000 hours of volunteering were undertaken on council land.

"To ensure volunteers can carry out their work safely on council land and indemnity insurance is provided we request that volunteers register with Cormac at volunteers@cormacltd.co.uk so we can give ongoing advice and support."

Resident Elz Ravenscroft asked Vernon if he would cut back the overgrown bushes on the pavement which her daughter used to walk to and from school.

"Jeremy has worked so hard for all of town and gone above and beyond for us all out of his own free time," she said.

"We're all so massively grateful for all his hard work and dedication to the town and town's people.

"From making the zigzag a safe space to walk through, to tidying up graffitied benches down the Ridgegrove to cut through a path."

She said: "The man honestly deserves so much recognition by the town council and beyond for all he's done."
